title: IP Routing & BGP Quick Revision
summary: Quick revision notes on how routers pick paths: routing tables, longest prefix match, default gateway and static routes, distance-vector vs link-state, OSPF and BGP with autonomous systems.

chapters.title: Routing Tables and the Mental Model
points: A routing table maps destination prefix → next hop + outgoing interface (+ metric); a router forwards each packet by looking up its destination IP, never by MAC
Route sources: connected (directly attached subnets), static (admin-typed), dynamic (learned via OSPF/BGP/etc.)
Forwarding is hop-by-hop: each router decides independently on its own table; the packet's IP stays the same while the L2 header is rewritten at each hop
Administrative distance ranks route sources when several protocols offer the same prefix: connected 0, static 1, eBGP 20, OSPF 110, RIP 120, iBGP 200 (lower wins)
Metric only compares routes within one protocol: RIP uses hop count, OSPF uses cost (based on bandwidth)

chapters.title: Longest Prefix Match, Default Gateway and Static Routes
points: Longest prefix match: of all routes containing the destination, the one with the longest mask (most specific) wins, regardless of metric or order; e.g. 10.1.1.0/24 beats 10.1.0.0/16 beats 0.0.0.0/0 for 10.1.1.5
Default route 0.0.0.0/0 matches everything with prefix length 0, so it is used only when nothing more specific matches (last resort)
Default gateway on a host is the router IP on its own subnet used for any destination outside that subnet; it must be in the host's subnet or traffic never leaves

Static route example: ip route add 10.2.0.0/16 via 192.168.1.1 (Linux) / ip route 10.2.0.0 255.255.0.0 192.168.1.1 (Cisco); it is not adapted automatically if the link fails, and a floating static route sets AD above the dynamic one (e.g. 200) as a backup
Common mistake: a route exists in one direction only, so packets arrive but replies have no return route; always verify both directions and that the next hop is reachable

chapters.title: Distance-Vector vs Link-State Routing
points: Distance-vector (RIP, EIGRP-like): each router shares its whole table of distances with neighbours only and learns the rest second-hand (routing by rumour)
Link-state (OSPF, IS-IS): each router floods link states (LSAs) to all routers in the area, builds an identical map (LSDB), and runs Dijkstra's SPF independently to compute shortest paths

Comparison: distance-vector has simple config and low CPU/memory but slow convergence and is prone to loops; link-state converges fast with a full topology view but needs more CPU/memory and design effort
Distance-vector pitfalls: count-to-infinity after a failure, countered by split horizon, poison reverse and a max hop limit (RIP: 15 is max, 16 is unreachable)
Path-vector (BGP) is a third type: it advertises the full AS path with each prefix, which prevents loops and lets policy be applied

chapters.title: OSPF Basics
points: OSPF is a link-state IGP using IP protocol 89, multicast 224.0.0.5 (all routers) and 224.0.0.6 (DR/BDR), with cost = reference bandwidth / interface bandwidth (default reference 100 Mbps, so raise it for 10G links)
Areas: Area 0 (backbone) is mandatory and all other areas must connect to it; areas limit LSA flooding and SPF scope; ABRs sit between areas
Neighbour states: Down → Init → 2-Way → ExStart → Exchange → Loading → Full; adjacency needs matching area ID, hello/dead timers (10s/40s on broadcast), subnet and authentication
On broadcast networks a Designated Router (DR) and Backup (BDR) are elected by highest priority, then highest router ID, to cut the number of adjacencies; election is non-preemptive

Cisco example: router ospf 1 / network 10.0.0.0 0.0.0.255 area 0; verify with show ip ospf neighbor and show ip route ospf (routes marked O), and stuck at Init or ExStart usually means a timer, MTU or area mismatch

chapters.title: BGP Basics and Autonomous Systems
points: An autonomous system (AS) is a set of networks under one administrative policy identified by an AS number (ASN); IGPs (OSPF) route inside an AS, BGP routes between ASes and carries the internet's routing table

BGP is a path-vector protocol over TCP port 179 with manually configured neighbours; it advertises prefixes with attributes, and a router rejects any route whose AS_PATH already contains its own ASN (loop prevention)

eBGP peers are in different ASes (AD 20, TTL 1 by default, directly connected); iBGP peers share an AS (AD 200), do not change the next hop by default, and need a full mesh or route reflectors because iBGP-learned routes are not re-advertised to other iBGP peers
Best-path order: highest weight (Cisco) → highest local preference → locally originated → shortest AS_PATH → lowest origin → lowest MED → eBGP over iBGP → lowest IGP metric to next hop

Example: router bgp 65001 / neighbor 203.0.113.2 remote-as 65002 / network 198.51.100.0 mask 255.255.255.0; the network statement only advertises a prefix already present in the routing table, and verify with show ip bgp summary (state Established, or Idle/Active means a TCP or config problem)

chapters.title: Routing Cheat Sheet
points: Lookup order: longest prefix first, then lowest administrative distance, then lowest metric; 0.0.0.0/0 is the last resort
Admin distance: connected 0, static 1, eBGP 20, OSPF 110, RIP 120, iBGP 200
Inspect tables: ip route / ip route get 8.8.8.8 (Linux), route print (Windows), show ip route (Cisco), traceroute to see each hop
Protocol picks: static for small or stub networks, OSPF inside an organisation, BGP between ASes and for multihoming to ISPs

Quick fixes: no connectivity outside the subnet → check default gateway; one-way traffic → check the return route; OSPF neighbour stuck → check area, timers, MTU, authentication; BGP not Established → check TCP 179 reachability, remote-as and ACLs
